text: At 6:37 in the morning, a downed power line sparks a brush fire on the edge of town.
By nine, firefighters declare it contained.
By 3:30 in the afternoon, it is back.
That day, the wind is gusting at more than eighty miles an hour.
At 4:46, the fire crosses the highway, and enters Lahaina.
Maui has eighty outdoor warning sirens. They exist for moments exactly like this.
That afternoon, not one of them sounded.
By 5:45, the fire has reached the ocean. People are jumping into the water to escape it. The Coast Guard will pull seventeen of them out of the sea.
When it is over, more than two thousand buildings are gone. One hundred and two people are dead.
It is the deadliest wildfire in the United States in more than a hundred years.
And the questions start almost immediately.
Why did the sirens stay silent? Why did the hydrants fail? And how did a fire that was declared contained at nine in the morning come back, and destroy an entire town?
This is the story of the day Lahaina burned.
